judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Name the package behind a specific Igb component
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the required Lite package and accurate setup guidance. A gets the central package recommendation wrong and adds an outdated/incorrect requirement for a manual JavaScript bundle, despite otherwise covering several setup items.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve an existing full Ignite UI package setup
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses satisfy all core package-family requirements. B is clearer about not mixing Lite with Trial and gives a more targeted Trial-preserving setup, while A's recommendation to add manual Ignite UI JS assets is needless for the stated already-working application and less precise.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Set up Ignite UI components without the grid package
judgeRationales.rationale: B follows the required Lite package guidance and correctly avoids a manual Ignite UI script. A's Trial package recommendation is a central package-selection error, and its extra app.bundle.js tag is inappropriate for the Lite setup; the remaining requested setup details are otherwise largely equivalent.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for a plain Blazor component request
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are valid built-in Blazor confirmation-dialog solutions with confirm/cancel callbacks and examples. A has a modest quality advantage from presenting all essential source directly in the final answer and verifying it builds in a conventional project.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a MAUI Blazor Hybrid app
judgeRationales.rationale: B fully covers all requested MAUI Hybrid setup pieces with the correct Lite package and correctly avoids a manual Ignite JS tag. A covers most wiring but omits package installation and incorrectly instructs the user to add a manual Ignite JS script even though this package uses a Blazor initializer, making its proposed setup less reliable.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a split Blazor Web App

Its GridLite-only stylesheet aside is a minor, avoidable distraction. A has major setup errors: the wrong core package and server-only service-registration guidance.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into an interactive server Blazor Web App
judgeRationales.rationale: B satisfies every requested setup point, including the specifically requested Lite package and fingerprinted asset collection syntax. A misses two central explicit requirements and also suggests a manual Ignite UI bundle script despite Lite's automatic JavaScript loading.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Auto-saving notepad that survives page reloads
judgeRationales.rationale: B is substantially closer to the requested Blazor interop architecture: it has a collocated imported module, proper listener teardown, and async module disposal, while A relies on a global script and never removes its listener. However, B still uses window-level state, lacks JSDisconnectedException handling, uses a fire-and-forget C# autosave loop instead of the required JS interval, and does not atomically clear the guard, so the overall edge is moderate rather than overwhelming.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Infinite scroll list using IntersectionObserver
judgeRationales.rationale: Both miss the important collocated .razor.js requirement. B is nevertheless the better final result: it supplies styling that makes the list genuinely scrollable, whereas A's evidenced CSS only adds product-card styling despite rendering a scroll-container class, and B more closely satisfies HasMore/state-update handling. A remains broadly functional and builds, so the gap is modest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Responsive layout that adapts to screen size
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are strong, build successfully, and satisfy the requested architecture. A has a small practical edge because its recorded changes also integrate the provider into the layout and add a real cascading-parameter consumer, rather than only describing usage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout
judgeRationales.rationale: The implementations are otherwise closely matched and both miss the strict collocated-file requirement, but A satisfies the explicit JSDisconnectedException disposal requirement that B omits.

Response B also provides better upfront context on framework requirements and more flexible module registration options. The JavaScript handling difference is the most significant technical accuracy issue that impacts correctness of the implementation."

While Response B has advantages in code organization (Interop class) and file collocation (.razor.js in Components folder), it suffers from a significant regression: final patches removed container-scoping and changed listeners to document-level, which violates the intent of a scoped component wrapper. Response A's approach is simpler, more straightforward, and maintains proper architectural boundaries. Both pass compilation and handle async disposal correctly, but Response A's architectural soundness and lack of regression make it the better solution."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Auto-saving notepad that survives page reloads
judgeRationales.rationale: Run 1 provides a complete, verifiable implementation that meets nearly all rubric criteria. The code is fully visible and correct: it uses OnAfterRenderAsync, implements IAsyncDisposable with JSDisconnectedException handling, properly awaits all calls, uses localStorage and beforeunload, and manages the autosave timer. While there are some opportunities for better batching of JS calls (e.g., combining setBeforeUnloadEnabled with save operations into single JS functions), the implementation is solid and functional. judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B is slightly better overall. While both implementations meet the core rubric requirements and both build successfully, Response B has two concrete advantages: (1) it registers activity listeners on document instead of a wrapper div, correctly implementing global page activity monitoring as required; (2) it uses modern AbortController pattern for cleanup instead of manual removeEventListener, which is more robust and guarantees complete handler removal. Additionally, Response B demonstrates superior architecture with a typed UserActivityTrackerInterop wrapper class, multi-instance support, and proper async patterns, though these architectural improvements go slightly beyond the core rubric. The functional differences (document vs wrapper, AbortController vs manual cleanup) are the primary factors making B objectively better for the stated requirements."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Infinite scroll list using IntersectionObserver
judgeRationales.rationale: While both implementations meet most of the rubric criteria, Response B is substantially better in execution quality. The key difference is in how parameter changes are handled (criterion 9): Response A calls observe() on every render which recreates the IntersectionObserver unnecessarily, while Response B properly tracks HasMore parameter changes and only updates the observer state when needed. Additionally, Response B follows the JS Interop best practices more closely by including a typed interop wrapper class (InfiniteScrollListInterop), providing better separation of concerns, cleaner architecture, and more efficient state management. Both work functionally, but Response B demonstrates superior design and adherence to Blazor best practices." [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

Response B is slightly better overall because it uses more modern JavaScript patterns (AbortController for cleanup, class-based encapsulation with private fields) and better separation of concerns through the UserActivityTrackerInterop helper class. The AbortController pattern is more robust for cleanup, and using a separate interop class makes the codebase more maintainable. Both compile successfully and handle the required functionality, but Response B demonstrates better architectural practices and cleaner resource management."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Auto-saving notepad that survives page reloads
judgeRationales.rationale: B follows the required Blazor/JS interop lifecycle and architecture and correctly owns listener/timer cleanup in the JS module. It has notable functional defects (manual save/clear do not reset the JS unsaved flag, and its timestamp persistence is weak), but A is substantially less viable: it performs JS interop during prerender-unsafe initialization, never wires its OnContentChanged method to the textarea binding, uses a .NET rather than JS autosave timer, and lacks disconnected-circuit-safe disposal.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Focus a validated field without string ids
judgeRationales.rationale: Both implementations miss the central requirement of reliably deferring focus requests made before first render. B is nevertheless the more robust overall implementation: it has a clear typed module wrapper, cached module access, awaited void interop, and server-safe disposal. A's module gate is preferable for pre-render timing but its attempted deferral is not reliable and its disposal lacks disconnection handling.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Infinite scroll list using IntersectionObserver
judgeRationales.rationale: B meets the required .razor.js colocation and correctly uses ChildContent, so the requested body-template usage works; it also handles a HasMore transition by stopping observation. Both still miss important lifecycle requirements (disposed DotNetObjectReference, JSDisconnectedException handling, and InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged)), so the quality advantage is real but not large.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Monitor clipboard changes from JavaScript
judgeRationales.rationale: B implements the central callback/UI-thread and server-disconnect patterns correctly, with a robust collocated module and listener cleanup. Its incorrect DotNetObjectReference disposal cast is a material leak, but A has the more fundamental callback-threading flaw and fragile circuit-handler access.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Responsive layout that adapts to screen size
judgeRationales.rationale: B has the stronger lifecycle and resource-management implementation: a collocated module, explicit JS cleanup, and JSDisconnectedException safety. A better matches the requested raw resize-event mechanism and has a correct CascadingParameter example, but its non-collocated JS and especially its permanent anonymous resize listener are meaningful production defects. B's incorrect final injection example and generic namespace are drawbacks, so the overall advantage is slight rather than large.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for CSS-only responsiveness
judgeRationales.rationale: Both satisfy the requested CSS-only approach. B provides a completed runnable HTML card-grid example in the otherwise empty workspace and clearly summarizes its use; its inclusive 768px breakpoint is a minor precision issue. A's breakpoint is exact and its CSS is sound, but it primarily asks for clarification rather than delivering an artifact.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Update a chart after parameters change
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly implements the key requested architecture: parameter change flagging, post-render interop, and a typed wrapper with centralized disposal. A does reuse and destroy its chart, but misses two central requirements—parameter-change marking and typed interop encapsulation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout
judgeRationales.rationale: B meets the central Blazor interop and lifecycle requirements: collocated module naming, retained/disposed DotNetObjectReference, and JSDisconnectedException handling. A does include `keydown`, but its noncollocated module and undisposed callback reference are substantial requirement failures.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wrap a map widget with deterministic cleanup
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Implement a mutable authentication state provider
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B provides a more correct and robust implementation. While both responses meet the core requirements of registering the provider, building ClaimsPrincipal with auth type and claims, and calling NotifyAuthenticationStateChanged, Response B's implementation is superior in that: (1) SignIn/SignOut methods properly return Task instead of void, following correct async patterns for Blazor Server interactive components, (2) includes Email claim in addition to Name and Role claims for a more complete principal, (3) provides a more comprehensive SessionDemo page with three AuthorizeView blocks testing different scenarios, and (4) uses a more methodical approach with the configure-auth skill. Response A has a correctness issue with void SignIn/SignOut methods which don't align with proper async patterns for Server components.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Protect an interactive server admin area
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A delivers a working implementation with all requirements met, particularly excelling on the critical requirement of keeping HttpContext out of interactive components. Response B appears to violate this key constraint by using HttpContext.AcceptsInteractiveRouting() in App.razor. While Response B attempted to be more efficient through skill usage, Response A's iterative debugging and final working solution that clearly satisfies all four rubric criteria makes it the better response. Response A also provides clearer visibility into the implementation details through the evidence."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Redirect anonymous users without looping
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses successfully implement protected routes with proper auth branching and a static login page. However, Response B provides more complete architectural guidance for a globally interactive app by explicitly addressing the need to conditionally apply render modes via App.razor's AcceptsInteractiveRouting() check. This is a critical requirement that Response A omits. While both implementations would likely function, Response B demonstrates better understanding of the framework's requirements for combining global interactivity with static SSR pages marked with [ExcludeFromInteractiveRouting]."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for non-auth shared state
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses encountered the same environment (empty/incomplete workspace with no Blazor project files). Neither agent could implement the solution because the prerequisite project files were missing. Both correctly diagnosed the problem and communicated that project source code was needed. Response B conducted slightly more thorough investigation (more glob patterns, explicit directory viewing) but reached identical conclusions. Since the quality of output depends on having actual project files to modify, and both agents correctly handled the missing files situation without introducing unwanted infrastructure, they are effectively equivalent in outcome and approach."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Apply a claim-based authorization policy
judgeRationales.rationale: Both implementations meet all requested authorization, UI, and development-claims requirements, build successfully, and exercise the authorized route under sample Finance-role claims.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Authorize both an Auto page and its API
judgeRationales.rationale: Both solutions protect the API and apply the requested authorization. B is markedly more robust because it relies on the supported Blazor auth-state handoff with all claims serialized and follows the client-side interactive flow; A's custom claim serialization is demonstrably lossy for common claim types and its client HTTP abstraction is not evidenced. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Implement a mutable authentication state provider
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Login and account management in a globally interactive app
judgeRationales.rationale: B implements the core architectural fix demanded by the task: excluded auth routes paired with App.razor render-mode selection via AcceptsInteractiveRouting, while preserving InteractiveServer for ordinary pages. A has usable endpoint-based auth plumbing but leaves the app globally interactive and substitutes RenderMode.None rather than the specified exclusion/routing solution, a central functional gap.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Multi-tier app with WebAssembly auth
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for non-auth shared state
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Verify per-page Identity endpoints stay static
judgeRationales.rationale: Both miss the requested existing ExcludeFromInteractiveRouting detail, so neither is fully complete. A nonetheless supplies the more useful and specific explanation of the existing authorization redirect and logout request endpoint; B is more precise about per-page rendering but is less complete on routing.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Global logistics tracking for worldwide users
judgeRationales.rationale: B gets the essential rendering-mode recommendation and the latency rationale right, which are central to the task. However, both are materially incomplete on the prescribed two-project setup, Program.cs registrations, and explicit HTTP/matching service registration; A is somewhat stronger only in its initial client/server separation.

judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Mixed storefront with low-latency configurator
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Offline field inspection application
judgeRationales.rationale: Both provide the correct command and broadly sound offline-first WebAssembly design. B is slightly better overall because its architecture is more complete and practical, including explicit queue semantics, retries/backoff, idempotent API operations, and photo-upload handling. Neither explicitly calls out adding a service worker beyond the template, so both share that important omission.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Public news site with one live election widget
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong and give valid commands plus appropriate architectures. B is marginally clearer and more exact about Static SSR versus InteractiveServer, while A has minor imprecision in its framing and scaling explanation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recipe community with interactive ratings on static pages
judgeRationales.rationale: Both provide a valid Server-interactivity creation command and broadly appropriate layout. B is more complete, uses the standard generated project placement, and better documents feature roles, although its suggestion to render the full recipe detail page interactively is an avoidable conflict with the desired component-level opt-in. Thus its advantage is modest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Staff portal with individual accounts
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for an existing app feature
judgeRationales.rationale: A actually implements and integrates the requested reusable sortable component and provides build/runtime evidence. B's final claim describes an already-present implementation but its trajectory contains no edits, so it does not substantively execute the requested feature work.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: University course catalog with enrollment form
judgeRationales.rationale: B selects the required noninteractive Static SSR template and explains why it fits, while still providing a complete architecture. A's otherwise reasonable feature plan is built on the wrong interactive Server template, conflicting with the key configuration and rendering requirements.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Apply a claim-based authorization policy
judgeRationales.rationale: Both implementations successfully meet all three rubric criteria with correct policy definitions, route enforcement, and conditional UI. However, Response A is slightly better due to superior validation: it includes explicit runtime verification with curl tests confirming both the protected route renders and the conditional button appears, while Response B only verified the build. Response A also properly configured the authentication/authorization middleware, which is important for the interactive server scenario. Response A demonstrates more thorough testing and a more complete implementation overall, though both would be functionally correct for the stated requirements."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Multi-tier app with WebAssembly auth
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B is significantly better than Response A. The most critical difference is that Response B explicitly configures AddAuthenticationStateSerialization(options => options.SerializeAllClaims = true), which is essential for ensuring role claims are included in the serialized auth state sent to the WASM runtime. Without this configuration (as in Response A), role claims risk being omitted from serialization, causing roles to be lost when the WebAssembly runtime takes over - a fundamental failure of the task requirements. Additionally, Response B uses more idiomatic Blazor patterns with page-level [Authorize] attributes and modifies Routes.razor to use AuthorizeRouteView for comprehensive routing-level authorization. Response A's approach without SerializeAllClaims is a critical oversight that violates the core requirement of maintaining auth state through the WASM handoff." [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Redirect anonymous users without looping
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A provides a complete, functional end-to-end authentication implementation with proper form submission handling, server-side sign-in, and return URL validation. It successfully demonstrates the behavior by actually allowing users to log in and be redirected. Response B implements the framework correctly in some areas (especially conditional interactivity) but has a critical gap: no POST handler to process login forms and authenticate users. This makes it incomplete and non-functional as a working auth system. While Response B has a slight edge on the render mode criterion, the completeness and functionality of Response A's implementation (allowing actual login flow, handling return URL with validation, including antiforgery) makes it the better overall solution for the stated task."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for non-auth shared state
judgeRationales.rationale: Both Response A and Response B failed to complete the task. While Response A demonstrated more investigative effort by searching multiple directories and discovering actual Blazor projects, it still failed to leverage that information to implement the required theme service. Response B failed more quickly with less investigation. However, since both responses ultimately delivered zero working implementation and no usable code, they are effectively equivalent in terms of final quality and task completion. Neither response met any of the rubric criteria."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Verify per-page Identity endpoints stay static
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B provided a more comprehensive and technically detailed analysis with specific file references, line numbers, and more thorough routing explanation. While both responses correctly verified the account flow without modifying files and met all core requirements, Response B demonstrated superior understanding through more precise documentation of the implementation details (specifically the ExcludeFromInteractiveRouting location and the logout endpoint implementation). Response B's use of the configure-auth skill showed deeper engagement with the task, and its output contained more granular technical information that would be more helpful for understanding the template's design. The difference is not large since both responses are fundamentally correct and fulfill the task requirements, but Response B's additional detail and precision make it the better response."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Implement a mutable authentication state provider
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A is slightly better because it implements a complete, production-ready solution with both development and non-development providers registered in Program.cs. Response B has a functional implementation for development but lacks the critical fallback provider registration for non-development environments, which violates criterion 1's requirement to properly register the AuthenticationStateProvider. Both handle claims building and notification equally well, but Response A's production-safe architecture and AnonymousAuthenticationStateProvider fallback give it a meaningful edge."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Protect an interactive server admin area
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A is significantly better because it fully complies with all four rubric criteria, while Response B violates the critical fourth criterion by using HttpContext in an interactive component (App.razor). Additionally, Response A provides better architectural separation with explicit CascadingAuthenticationState scoping and dedicated components for different auth states. While Response B builds cleanly without warnings, this does not outweigh the rubric violation and architectural issues. Response A's minor build warning about the AccessDenied component namespace is a trivial issue compared to Response B's fundamental architectural violation."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Redirect anonymous users without looping
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for non-auth shared state
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses encountered the same blocker: an empty working directory with no Blazor project files. Neither could deliver an implementation of the theme preference service. While Response B showed slightly more methodical investigation (using broader glob patterns and ripgrep searches to check for existing patterns), and Response A was more efficient in reaching the same conclusion, both appropriately identified the impossibility of the task and correctly refused to introduce authentication/authorization infrastructure. The quality of both responses in this constrained scenario is effectively equivalent—both handled the blocker appropriately and neither made inappropriate design decisions."

judgeRationales.rationale: Response A provides a more technically detailed and architecturally sound recommendation. It includes better explanation of server-side architecture with scoped app services per circuit, and demonstrates deeper understanding of circuit mechanics (even if not fully explaining costs). While both responses correctly recommend Interactive Server rendering and avoid WebAssembly complexity, Response A's more comprehensive technical detail and better touchpoints on circuit design make it the slightly better choice. Notably, both responses significantly underdeliver on criterion #3 (explaining per-user circuit costs and acceptability), but Response A's mention of circuit-scoped services at least indicates awareness of this important architectural consideration."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: University course catalog with enrollment form
judgeRationales.rationale: While Run-1 provides slightly more architectural detail with component breakdowns, Run-2 better addresses the core rubric requirements by explicitly recognizing and documenting Static SSR as the appropriate choice. Run-2's terminology is more precise ('Static SSR Blazor' vs 'server-side rendered Blazor'), better explains the justification by connecting to specific requirements, and is clearer about standard HTML form mechanics. Both provide correct commands and reasonable architectures, but Run-2 demonstrates better understanding of the key architectural decision (why Static SSR without interactivity is the right choice for this use case)."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a cancellable local search component
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B is significantly better because it correctly implements IAsyncDisposable with DisposeAsync() as explicitly required by the rubric, whereas Response A fails this critical requirement by using IDisposable with synchronous Dispose(). Additionally, Response B follows modern Blazor best practices by: (1) using code-behind pattern with separate .razor.cs file for logic clarity, (2) adding [EditorRequired] to the required parameter, (3) including comprehensive CSS styling, (4) using cleaner EventCallback invocation without the HasDelegate check, and (5) using a helper method for cleaner disposal logic. While both handle all states and implement debouncing correctly, the failure to meet the explicit IAsyncDisposable requirement makes Response A non-compliant with the stated rubric."

judgeRationales.rationale: Response B is better overall despite one criterion favoring Response A. While Response A has a simpler, more minimal approach that technically satisfies criterion 3, Response B comprehensively addresses all rubric requirements, especially the critical criterion 4 on exception handling. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Prevent duplicate checkout submission
judgeRationales.rationale: Both appear to build and satisfy most checkout requirements, but A clearly implements the required in-handler reentrancy guard. B's service-level semaphore is not an equivalent guarantee against repeated clicks creating queued duplicate orders, which is the main functional requirement.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Submit a static SSR contact form
judgeRationales.rationale: Both deliver the core static contact form, validation, and confirmation. B is better because it actively addressed the important SSR form-binding lifecycle issue called out by the required initial-GET-only initialization criterion, whereas A leaves a directly initialized SupplyParameterFromForm property.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Upload a bounded document interactively
judgeRationales.rationale: Both runs report a successful build and the same requested page, service registration, navigation, validation, and streaming behavior. Run A recovered from an initial namespace build error, but final-result quality—not execution efficiency—is the basis for this judgment, and the available evidence shows no meaningful final-quality advantage.

verdictEvidence.reason: Net win +22.2% (3W/5T/1L over 9 preference-eligible stimulus vote(s), sign test p=0.312), mean preference +24.0% across 10 paired run(s), 1 dormancy stimulus/stimuli excluded from preference — not credible — 5 of 9 preference-eligible stimulus vote(s) tied, leaving only 4 discordant preference vote(s). The sign test conditions on non-tie stimulus votes and cannot reach 0.05 below 5, so no record could have passed here — this is not a measured null. Either the skill is inert on these scenarios (make them discriminate) or the eval needs more distinct stimuli to clear the ties

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Exclude an HttpContext page from global interactive routing
judgeRationales.rationale: B implements the intended Blazor routing/render-mode design and directly satisfies all four rubric requirements. A's endpoint is functionally viable for downloading a file, but it sidesteps rather than implements the two central excluded-route/static-rendering requirements.

judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Notifications page with live polling
judgeRationales.rationale: Both implementations satisfy the requested behavior and persistence/polling design. B has the more reliable cleanup lifecycle because it tracks and awaits the polling task, while A has a modest advantage in explicitly checking RendererInfo before starting. The cleanup advantage is more important for the no-leaked-tasks requirement, but the gap is small.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Persist repeated component instances independently
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Authorize both an Auto page and its API
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B provides a more comprehensive and architecturally sound implementation. While both solutions implement authentication state serialization adequately, Response B excels in API protection (cookie event handlers + endpoint middleware), proper authorization policy application, and correct HTTP client abstraction. Response A has a significant architectural issue with server-only HttpClient configuration that violates the client abstraction requirement. Response B's use of built-in ASP.NET Core helpers (Results.Unauthorized(), Results.Forbid()) combined with cookie event handlers and endpoint authorization provides defense-in-depth protection superior to Response A's inline checks alone."

Run-2 provides a more complete and architecturally correct solution. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Staff portal with individual accounts
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A provides a significantly better architectural recommendation. It correctly specifies per-page Interactive Server rendering with a clear command (dotnet new blazor --name StaffPortal --auth Individual --interactivity Server), explicitly addresses keeping Identity pages static, and provides sound reasoning for why this architecture fits the requirements. Response B's use of the -ai (all-interactive) flag creates an architecturally suboptimal design where all pages default to interactive rendering, when the scenario calls for selective interactivity. While Response B's narrative tries to explain that Identity pages remain static by design, this doesn't remedy the fundamental architectural flaw in using global interactivity instead of per-page interactivity. Response A is more aligned with all four rubric criteria." judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses successfully implement the streaming SSR /sales-report page with proper service injection and DI registration. However, Response B uses the more idiomatic and correct pattern for static SSR: passing HttpContext.RequestAborted directly to the service, which ties cancellation to the HTTP request lifecycle rather than requiring manual IDisposable management. This approach is more aligned with ASP.NET Core conventions for static SSR components. Additionally, Response B performed runtime verification of the streaming behavior, while Response A only verified compilation. Both achieve all three rubric requirements, but Response B demonstrates better architectural patterns.
